findings.title: IMSI Catcher — Excessive IMSI Identity Requests
findings.description: 3 IMSI Identity Requests (identity type 1) detected within a 120-second window. Normal LTE operation requires ≤2 Identity Requests. This pattern is a primary signature of active IMSI catcher operation targeting subscriber identity.
findings.technique: IMSI Harvesting via Identity Request Flood
findings.hardware_hint: Active IMSI catcher (IMSI grabber / Stingray / Cobham / Septier)
findings.recommended_action:
1. Preserve all NDJSON/QMDL files with SHA-256 manifest.
2. Document exact timestamps for legal evidence.
3. Reference 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.4.4 (Identity Procedure).
4. Submit to ACMA under Radiocommunications Act 1992 s.189.
5. Include in AFP/ACORN referral as primary IMSI catcher evidence.

findings.title: CRITICAL: Full Null-Cipher Attack (EEA0 + EIA0)
findings.description:
1 Security Mode Command(s) negotiated with EEA0 (no encryption) AND EIA0 (no integrity protection). This violates 3GPP TS 33.401 §5.1.3.2 which prohibits EIA0 in normal operation. Traffic is transmitted in PLAINTEXT with no tamper detection. This is the signature of a Man-in-the-Middle attack by a rogue base station.

NOTE: If running against M7350 dual-unit captures from the Cranbourne East investigation (January 2026 onwards), zero EEA0 events are expected — Harris Transparent Proxy mode uses EEA2/EIA2. Verify against raw tshark output before submitting.
findings.hardware_hint: Rogue eNodeB / IMSI catcher with active MitM capability (Stingray, Cobham UMTS/LTE, Septier IMSI Catcher, or similar). NOTE: Harris commercial devices in Transparent Proxy mode do NOT produce EEA0 — if this fires on Cranbourne East data it is likely a false positive from UE capability fields. Verify with tshark.
findings.recommended_action:
VERIFY FIRST: Run tshark -r <file> -Y 'lte_rrc.SecurityModeCommand_element' -T fields -e lte_rrc.cipheringAlgorithm to confirm EEA0 in actual SMC.

If confirmed:
1. Preserve QMDL files — the SecurityModeCommand is logged with timestamp.
2. Cross-reference timestamps with known rogue cell activity.
3. Cite 3GPP TS 33.401 §5.1.3.2 in ACMA complaint.
4. Submit to AFP/ACORN with SecurityModeCommand decoded packet as exhibit.

findings.title: Forced 2G Downgrade (GERAN Redirect in RRC Release)
findings.description: 1 RRC Connection Release message(s) contained a GERAN (GSM/2G) redirected carrier. This forces the device to drop to 2G where GSM's A5/1 cipher (or A5/0 — no cipher) is trivially broken. This is a classic IMSI catcher downgrade attack.
findings.technique: LTE→2G Forced Downgrade via GERAN Redirect
findings.hardware_hint: Rogue LTE eNodeB with 2G fallback — forces victim to 2G where a paired GSM IMSI catcher operates
findings.recommended_action:
1. Document the RRC Connection Release packet with GERAN IEs.
2. Note the target ARFCN — correlate with GSM scan data.
3. This is a two-stage attack: LTE rogue → forced 2G → passive intercept.
4. Alert: Do not use voice calls or SMS while this is active.

findings.title: IMSI-Targeted Paging Detected
findings.description: 3 Paging message(s) used IMSI as the paging identity. 3GPP TS 24.301 requires networks to use S-TMSI for paging in LTE. IMSI-targeted paging reveals the subscriber's permanent identity and is used by IMSI catchers to locate a specific target subscriber.
findings.recommended_action:
1. This is a direct violation of 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.6.2.
2. Document paging channel content and timestamps.
3. IMSI-paging combined with forced downgrade = location tracking chain.
4. Report to ACMA and include in AFP referral.

findings.title: IMSI Paging Within 30s of Identity Request
findings.description: IMSI-targeted paging occurred within 30 seconds of an Identity Request. This sequence: Identity Request → IMSI harvest → IMSI-targeted paging confirms active subscriber tracking — the attacker is confirming device location after harvesting IMSI.
findings.technique: IMSI Harvest → Location Confirmation (correlated event chain)
findings.recommended_action: This correlated event chain (Identity Request → IMSI Paging) is the strongest possible indicator of active targeting. Submit as primary evidence to AFP.

findings.title: Cell 98765 Observed on Multiple EARFCNs: 1450, 9350
findings.description: Cell ID 98765 was observed operating on 2 different EARFCNs: 1450, 9350. A legitimate LTE cell transmits on exactly one EARFCN (primary frequency). Simultaneous multi-EARFCN operation from a single Cell ID is a strong indicator of a rogue base station using software-defined radio with a spoofed Cell ID.
findings.technique: Multi-EARFCN Cell Operation (rogue SDR base station signature)
findings.hardware_hint: SDR-based rogue eNodeB (e.g., srsRAN/OpenAirInterface on USRP/HackRF) broadcasting a spoofed Cell ID across multiple frequencies.
findings.recommended_action:
1. This is one of the strongest rogue tower indicators.
2. Document each EARFCN → Cell ID pairing with timestamps.
3. Cross-reference EARFCNs against Rayhunter Unit 2 data.
4. A real cell has one EARFCN — multiple EARFCNs = fake cell.
5. Include as primary exhibit in ACMA / AFP submissions.

findings.title: IMEISV Device Fingerprinting Detected — 1 Event(s)
findings.description: 1 NAS Identity Request(s) for IMEISV (identity type 3) observed. The device attached using a GUTI (temporary identity — no IMSI exposed on attach), but the rogue cell subsequently demanded the IMEISV: the device's hardware fingerprint (IMEI + software version). This uniquely identifies the specific physical handset. Legitimate networks do not request IMEISV during normal operation — this is targeted device identification. Confirmed via tshark on raw PCAPNG binary (1778156124.pcapng): frames 650, 1098, 1970, 2639 all decode as msg_emm_type=0x55, id_type2=IMEISV (3). Source: 3GPP TS 24.301 §5.4.4.3.
findings.hardware_hint: Harris commercial IMSI catcher — IMEISV collection after GUTI-based attach is consistent with Harris Transparent Proxy mode. Device could not obtain IMSI via attach (GUTI used), so fell back to IMEISV demand.
findings.recommended_action:
IMEISV collection without lawful authority may violate the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 (Cth) s.7.
1. Document frame numbers and timestamps.
2. Note that phone used GUTI on attach — rogue cell actively demanded IMEISV.
3. Include in ACMA ENQ-1851DVJH04 and AFP complaint.
4. Cross-reference with UEInformationRequest-r9 events in same session.

findings.title: Identity Request Following Authentication Reject
findings.description: A 1×IMEI/IMEISV Identity Request was sent within 10 seconds of an Authentication Reject. This is a known IMSI catcher technique: reject authentication to force the UE to reveal its identity.
findings.hardware_hint: Active IMSI catcher (auth reject + re-request pattern)
findings.recommended_action: This sequence is a textbook Stingray attack. Preserve evidence.

findings.title: Unprovoked Identity Request — No Prior Attach
findings.description: 1×IMEI/IMEISV, 3×IMSI Identity Request(s) observed with no preceding Attach or Tracking Area Update Request. Legitimate networks only request identity during attach procedures. Unprovoked requests indicate a rogue device is probing for subscriber or device identity.
findings.hardware_hint: Rogue base station (IMSI catcher in active mode)
findings.recommended_action: Cross-reference with cell ID and timing to locate transmitter.

findings.title: Security Mode Command Without Prior Authentication
findings.description: Security Mode Command observed with no preceding Authentication Request/Response sequence. Legitimate LTE authentication must precede security mode setup. This indicates a rogue device skipping authentication to negotiate cipher parameters with an unauthenticated identity.
findings.recommended_action: Cross-reference with Identity Request events. No-auth → SMC combined with EEA0 is definitive IMSI catcher evidence.

findings.title: LTE ProSe Proximity Config (reportProximityConfig-r9) — flag only, IE not decoded
findings.description: 1 RRC message(s) flagged with ProSe proximity reporting. Set from a parser flag without confirming the reportProximityConfig-r9 IE in the decode — verify before citing.
evidence: [2026-03-31T14:00:50+00:00] RRC Connection Reconfiguration targetPCI=? EARFCN=?  PROSE=YES (synthetic_test.ndjson)
findings.hardware_hint: Modified eNodeB with ProSe capability (if IE confirmed).
findings.recommended_action:
1. Decode the RRC frame and confirm reportProximityConfig-r9 is present.
2. Only cite as tracking if the IE is in the decode, not just the flag.
